title: CSC 2770 Module 5: Networking Essentials
source: Networking Essentials slides, CSC 2770: Introduction to Systems and Networking (Jacob Strickler)

questions.q: What is a network?
choices: A collection of interconnected devices that communicate and/or share resources
A group of computers that share a single connection to the Internet
Any set of devices that is owned and managed by one organization
The physical cables and wireless signals that link devices together
questions.explain: A network is interconnected devices that communicate and/or share resources. It doesn't have to reach the Internet. Single ownership describes a LAN, and the cables and signals are the physical medium, not the network itself.

questions.q: End devices are devices that:
choices: Are the source or the destination of communication across a network
Provide the infrastructure that lets other devices communicate
Sit at the edge of a WAN and connect it to the Internet
Translate data between digital and analog formats
questions.explain: End devices are where communication starts or ends. Many of them are devices users interact with directly. Providing the infrastructure that connects devices is what intermediary devices do, and digital/analog translation is the modem's job.

questions.q: Which best describes intermediary devices?
choices: Infrastructure that enables end devices to communicate
Devices that are the source or destination of communication
Devices that users interact with directly, like laptops
Wearable and medical devices that sit on or in the body
questions.explain: Intermediary devices (modems, routers, switches, hubs, ...) are the infrastructure that lets end devices communicate. They make larger and long-distance networks possible.

questions.q: Which of these are end devices?
questions.explain: The refrigerator (IoT), file server, insulin pump (personal medical device) and printer are each the source or destination of data. Switches, modems and hubs pass data along, so they are intermediary devices.

questions.q: A server is an intermediary device, because it serves data to other machines on the network.
questions.explain: Servers are end devices. Data starts or ends at a server; it doesn't pass through one on its way somewhere else.

questions.q: Only general-purpose computers such as desktops, laptops, phones and servers can be part of a network. Appliances like lights and refrigerators cannot.
questions.explain: Almost anything can be on a network. IoT devices such as smart TVs, lights and refrigerators are end devices, and so are wearables and medical devices such as pacemakers.

questions.q: A pacemaker sends heart-rhythm readings to the patient's smartphone. In this exchange, the pacemaker is:
questions.explain: The pacemaker is where the data comes from (its source), which makes it an end device. Personal medical devices such as pacemakers, insulin pumps and glucose monitors are all end devices.

questions.q: The Internet is an example of which type of network?
questions.explain: The Internet is a Wide Area Network. It spans cities, states, countries and continents and connects many smaller networks.

questions.q: A military base links the LANs in its many buildings into one larger network. What type of network is this?
questions.explain: A CAN is several connected LANs serving a larger site, such as a university campus, military base, large medical complex or shopping mall. CANs and MANs are 'LANs of LANs'.

questions.q: A city builds a network that connects its residents, school systems, public services and emergency responders. Which type of network is it?
questions.explain: A MAN serves an entire city or part of a city. A WAN would span multiple cities, states, countries or continents.

questions.q: In this module, the M in MAN stands for:
questions.explain: The slides spell it Municipal Area Network. Many other sources say Metropolitan Area Network, which means the same thing: a city-scale network.

questions.q: Your smartwatch syncs step counts over Bluetooth to the phone in your pocket. What kind of network is this?
questions.explain: A PAN is a very small network, a few square feet at most, that connects one person's devices using short-range technology such as Bluetooth. A worn device like the watch may also be described as part of a BAN (Body Area Network).

questions.q: A network counts as a LAN only if it stays under a fixed maximum number of devices.
questions.explain: A LAN has no strict size limit. It is generally confined to a small number of buildings and owned and managed by a single entity, such as one person, one company or one administration.

questions.q: Which description fits a typical LAN?
choices: Confined to a few buildings and managed by a single entity
Spans several countries and relies on satellite links
Limited to a few square feet and one person's devices
Covers a whole city and connects its public services
questions.explain: Examples of LANs are a home (devices connected via a modem and router), a local office and a public school. The other choices describe a WAN, a PAN and a MAN.

questions.q: Which short-range technologies are PANs generally connected with?
questions.explain: PANs use short-range technologies: Bluetooth, IR and NFC. Cellular and satellite links cover long distances, and coaxial cable is a wired medium.

questions.q: Which ordering runs from smallest to largest scope?
choices: BAN < PAN < LAN < CAN < MAN < WAN
PAN < BAN < LAN < MAN < CAN < WAN
BAN < PAN < CAN < LAN < MAN < WAN
PAN < LAN < BAN < CAN < WAN < MAN
questions.explain: The full nesting from the diagram is Nano < BAN < PAN < LAN < CAN < MAN < RAN < WAN. A BAN sits inside a PAN, and CANs and MANs are built from LANs.

questions.q: In the nested-circle diagram of network types, which type sits between MAN and WAN?
questions.explain: Nano < BAN < PAN < LAN < CAN < MAN < RAN < WAN. RAN is commonly expanded as Regional Area Network, a scale between a city and a WAN.

questions.q: WANs rely on what kind of infrastructure?
choices: Permanent, reliable links such as copper/fiber cable and satellites
Short-range links such as Bluetooth, infrared and NFC
A single shared cable that every device taps into
Hubs that repeat each message to every connected device
questions.explain: WANs connect many LANs and other smaller networks over very large distances, so they rely on more permanent and/or reliable infrastructure: cable (copper, fiber optic, etc.) and satellites.

questions.q: A company with offices on three continents connects them all, and its employees also log in remotely from home. What type of network does this require?
questions.explain: Corporations with distant offices, remote employees, cloud services and anything else that needs connectivity over very large distances use WANs.

questions.q: Which cable carries light signals through glass or plastic fibers?
questions.explain: Fiber optic cable carries light. Coaxial cable is a conductor inside a metallic shield, and twisted pair (Cat5e, Cat6, etc.) is copper wire twisted together.

questions.q: Which cable is a conducting cable surrounded by a metallic shield?
questions.explain: Coaxial cable has a central conductor surrounded by a metallic shield.

questions.q: Cat5e and Cat6 are examples of which medium?
questions.explain: Cat5e and Cat6 are twisted pair cables, made of copper wires twisted together. This is ordinary Ethernet cable.

questions.q: Wireless links such as Wi-Fi don't count as a physical medium, since nothing tangible connects the devices.
questions.explain: Wireless counts as a physical medium. It is intangible media (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, IR, Zigbee, cellular), as opposed to tangible media such as cables.

questions.q: Which of these are intangible (wireless) media?
questions.explain: The intangible media listed are Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Infrared (IR), Zigbee and cellular. Coax, fiber and twisted pair are tangible (wired) media.

questions.q: Wireless media generally rely on:
choices: Light pulses sent through glass fibers
Electrical current in twisted copper pairs
A token passed from device to device
questions.explain: Wireless media generally use radio waves or electromagnetic radiation. Light through glass fibers describes fiber optic cable, copper pairs describe twisted pair, and the token belongs to ring topologies.

questions.q: Regardless of a network's size, every device on it must be connected through some physical medium.
questions.explain: Every network, from a PAN to a WAN, needs a physical medium. It can be tangible (cables) or intangible (wireless).

questions.q: The layout of connections between devices on a network is called its:
questions.explain: Network topology is the layout of connections between devices. Scope is the area or purpose a network covers (PAN, LAN, WAN...), and the medium is what carries the signal.

questions.q: Devices on a network are called nodes. What other term, borrowed from graph theory, is used for a node? (one word)
questions.explain: Nodes are also called vertices (singular: vertex), and connections are also called edges or links.

questions.q: Connections between nodes may also be called:
questions.explain: A connection is the medium through which nodes communicate. Depending on context it is also called an edge or a link. Vertex is the other name for a node.

questions.q: Fault tolerance refers to a network's:
choices: Ability to keep working when components are compromised
Speed at which packets can be sent across it
Ease of being expanded to more devices
Rate of collisions on shared channels
questions.explain: Fault tolerance is the capacity to keep functioning when components are compromised, e.g. a broken connection. Packet speed and collisions are part of performance, and ease of expansion is scalability.

questions.q: Performance refers to:
choices: Speed and efficiency: packet speed, latency, collisions
Continuing to work after a connection breaks
How cheaply and quickly the network can grow
How readily the network can be expanded
questions.explain: Performance is the speed and efficiency of the network: how quickly packets can be sent across it, how much latency there is, how many collisions occur, etc.

questions.q: Scalability can consider both the overhead of expanding a network (cost, complexity, downtime) and how the network behaves once it is larger.
questions.explain: Scalability is how readily a network can be expanded. It can mean the overhead of expanding and/or the network's behavior (performance, fault tolerance, etc.) at the larger size.

questions.q: A bus is cheap and quick to extend, yet its performance drops noticeably as devices are added. What does this show about scalability?
choices: Low expansion overhead can coexist with poor behavior at scale
Scalability depends only on the cost of adding devices
A topology that is easy to expand always performs well
Scalability and performance are unrelated properties
questions.explain: Scalability has two sides: the overhead of expanding and how the network behaves at the new size. A bus does well on the first and badly on the second.

questions.q: What is a collision?
choices: Devices on a shared channel transmitting at the same time
A packet arriving at the wrong destination address
A cable break that disconnects one device
Two devices being assigned the same IP address
questions.explain: A collision happens when devices that share a communication channel transmit at once and interfere. That is why collisions are a problem on shared media (bus, hub) and why a ring uses a token.

questions.q: Which topology links exactly two devices with a direct connection between them?
questions.explain: Point-to-point is the most basic physical topology: exactly two devices and one direct link.

questions.q: Why does a point-to-point network generally have high performance?
choices: Nothing competes for bandwidth and no middle devices add latency
A token stops the two devices from transmitting at once
Traffic is spread across many redundant connections
A central node schedules traffic between the devices
questions.explain: With only two devices on one link, nothing else competes for bandwidth, and there are no intermediate devices to create latency.

questions.q: A point-to-point network has nonexistent fault tolerance: either both devices and the link work, or the network fails.
questions.explain: There is no alternate path or device, so any single failure takes down the whole network.

questions.q: A point-to-point topology scales well, because a third device can simply be added to the same direct link.
questions.explain: Point-to-point topologies do not scale, by definition. Adding a third device turns it into a different topology.

questions.q: A bus topology connects many devices through:
choices: A single shared medium, such as one cable
A central node with one link per device
Direct links between every pair of devices
A closed loop that passes a token around
questions.explain: A bus uses one shared medium. A central node describes a star, links between every pair describe a full mesh, and a closed loop with a token describes a ring.

questions.q: What happens to a bus network's performance as more devices are added?
choices: It decreases noticeably, as all devices share one medium
It increases, because each new device adds another path
It stays the same, since the cable's speed is fixed
It improves, because the token prevents collisions
questions.explain: Every device on a bus competes for the same single medium, so performance drops noticeably as devices are added. Buses don't use a token; rings do.

questions.q: Which of these are advantages of a bus topology?
choices: Performance holds steady as devices are added
questions.explain: A bus is extremely simple: quick to set up, needs minimal resources and is easily expanded. But it has little fault tolerance, and performance decreases as devices are added.

questions.q: A designer needs the simplest, quickest setup with minimal resources for several devices, and reliability is not a concern. Which topology fits best?
questions.explain: A bus is simple, quick to set up and needs minimal resources. The trade-off is little fault tolerance, and performance drops as more devices are added. A full mesh is the most complex and costly option.

questions.q: A ring topology is essentially:
choices: A bus with its two ends connected
A star with a backup central node
A mesh with one link per device
A pair of devices joined by one direct link
questions.explain: A ring is a bus whose ends are joined. Depending on its structure, data travels in one direction or both.

questions.q: In a ring topology, what does the token do?
choices: Grants permission to transmit, which helps prevent collisions
Encrypts data as it passes each device on the ring
Converts data between digital and analog formats
Records the MAC address of each device it visits
questions.explain: The token works like a 'talking stick'. At each device it checks whether that device needs to transmit. If so, the device transmits; if not, the token moves on. Only one device sends at a time, which helps prevent collisions.

questions.q: Compared with a unidirectional ring, a bidirectional ring has:
choices: Greater fault tolerance and lower latency
Lower cost and fewer cables to install
No need for a token to avoid collisions
Unlimited scalability with no extra overhead
questions.explain: In a bidirectional ring data can travel either way around, so there are multiple channels. That gives greater fault tolerance and lower latency.

questions.q: A unidirectional ring has the same general downsides as a bus.
questions.explain: With data going only one way around, a unidirectional ring behaves much like a bus: little fault tolerance and limited performance.

questions.q: Which topology is essentially many point-to-point links from one central device?
questions.explain: In a star, every device has its own link to a central node, so it is like many point-to-point links radiating from one device.

questions.q: In a star network, the cable to one workstation is cut. What happens?
choices: Only that workstation loses its connection
The network falls back to a ring topology
questions.explain: Each device has its own link, so a single broken link does not disable the whole network. Links have no redundancy, though, so that one device is cut off.

questions.q: What is the single point of failure in a star topology?
choices: The device farthest from the center
questions.explain: All traffic passes through the central device. If it fails, the whole network goes down.

questions.q: In a star topology, devices communicate directly with one another and use the central node only as a backup.
questions.explain: Devices in a star never communicate directly. Everything goes through the central node, which acts as the intermediary.

questions.q: Which topology has the highest fault tolerance?
questions.explain: A mesh has so many links that almost any point of failure can be routed around. A full mesh, where every device links to every other, has the most redundancy.

questions.q: What is the main drawback of a mesh topology?
choices: Cost, complexity and connection overhead make scaling hard
A central device is a single point of failure
Every device competes for one shared cable
Data can travel in only one direction
questions.explain: Meshes are more complex, more costly and need immense overhead for connections, so scalability can be a problem. A single point of failure is the star's weakness, and one shared cable is the bus's.

questions.q: Why does a mesh topology tend to increase overall performance?
choices: Traffic can be spread across many different connections
A single token keeps any two devices from colliding
All traffic passes through one fast central node
Every device shares one high-speed cable
questions.explain: With many links available, traffic can be distributed across different connections instead of competing for one path.

questions.q: A full mesh connects 8 devices, each linked directly to every other device. How many links does it need?
questions.explain: Each of the n devices links to the other n - 1, and each link is shared by two devices, so there are n(n - 1)/2 links: 8 x 7 / 2 = 28. (The 6-node full mesh in the slide diagram has 6 x 5 / 2 = 15.) This fast growth is the 'immense overhead' that makes meshes hard to scale.

questions.q: In a partial mesh, every device is connected to every other device.
questions.explain: That describes a full mesh. In a partial mesh, each device connects to as many nodes as is reasonable.

questions.q: In the hybrid-topology example of a university network, which topology connects the departments/buildings, and which is used inside each building?
choices: Mesh between buildings; star inside each
Star between buildings; mesh inside each
Bus between buildings; ring inside each
Ring between buildings; bus inside each
questions.explain: A mesh between buildings keeps campus-wide communication consistent and redundant. Inside each building, a star connects workstations to a central access point.

questions.q: In the university hybrid example, the star topology inside each building is chosen mainly to provide:
choices: Better control and scalability within that building
A direct link between every pair of workstations
questions.explain: The star gives better control and scalability within the building. Consistent, redundant campus-wide communication is what the mesh between buildings provides.

questions.q: In practice, most networks use a single pure topology, such as a star or a bus.
questions.explain: Most real networks are hybrid topologies: mixtures of several topologies, often organized into layers and hierarchies. The right structure depends on the network's size, purpose and the devices it connects.

questions.q: What does a modem do?
choices: Translates data between digital and analog formats
Routes packets to destinations using IP addresses
Forwards local traffic using MAC addresses
Repeats incoming data to every local device
questions.explain: A modem translates between digital data (what computers understand) and analog signals (what can travel along cables and phone lines), and back again. Computers and the Internet's lines 'speak different languages', and the modem is the translator. The other choices describe a router, a switch and a hub.

questions.q: How do digital and analog signals differ?
choices: Digital: light pulses; analog: radio waves
Digital: MAC addresses; analog: IP addresses
questions.explain: Digital signals are binary values (0 or 1). Analog infrastructure carries waves, as audio does.

questions.q: Analog signals are subject to noise and distortion.
questions.explain: Analog signals are waves, and noise and distortion can corrupt them in transmission.

questions.q: Which pairing is correct?
choices: Switch: MAC addresses, layer 2; router: IP addresses, layer 3
Switch: IP addresses, layer 3; router: MAC addresses, layer 2
Switch: MAC addresses, layer 3; router: IP addresses, layer 2
Switch: IP addresses, layer 2; router: MAC addresses, layer 3
questions.explain: Switches use MAC addresses and operate at the Data Link layer (layer 2) of the OSI model. Routers use IP addresses and operate at the Network layer (layer 3).

questions.q: Switches operate at which layer of the OSI model? Give the layer's name.
questions.explain: Switches work at the Data Link layer (layer 2) and use MAC addresses. Routers work at the Network layer (layer 3) and use IP addresses.

questions.q: Which of these are jobs a router does?
choices: Routing packets to their appropriate destinations
Tracking devices on the network by IP address
Translating digital data into analog signals
Repeating every message to all local devices
questions.explain: When several devices share a connection to a larger network such as the Internet, the router tracks them by IP address and sends traffic to the right one. Routers also provide Wi-Fi. Digital-to-analog translation is the modem's job, and repeating to everyone is how a hub works.

questions.q: An office wants its workstations and printers to talk to each other quickly and directly, without going through a router or a wider network, and without broadcasting every message to every device. Which device fits?
questions.explain: A switch handles traffic inside the local network, without connecting to a larger network, and delivers data to the intended device by MAC address. A hub would broadcast everything to everyone.

questions.q: A hub receives data meant for one device on the local network. What does it do next?
choices: Repeats it to all devices on the local network
Looks up the recipient's MAC address and sends it there
Forwards it to the router using the recipient's IP
Converts it to analog and sends it to the modem
questions.explain: The steps are: a device sends data to the hub, the hub repeats it to all local devices, the intended recipient processes it, and the other devices ignore it. Sending only to the right MAC address is what a switch does.

questions.q: After a hub broadcasts data, what do the devices that are not the intended recipient do with it?
choices: Send it back to the hub
questions.explain: Only the intended recipient processes the data. Every other device ignores it, so most of the traffic a hub creates is unnecessary.

questions.q: Why is a hub inefficient?
choices: Most of the communication it causes is unnecessary
It has no filtering or addressing mechanism
Collisions are more likely because all devices share one channel
It must translate every message from digital to analog
It only works across a WAN
questions.explain: A hub sends everything to everyone. Most of that traffic is unnecessary, the hub has no filtering or addressing, and because all devices share one communication channel, collisions are much more likely.

questions.q: A hub is an outdated device that did a switch's job before switches were widely available.
questions.explain: Hubs did the switch's job before switches were available and widely used. They broadcast every message instead of delivering it to the intended device.

questions.q: A switch connects the local network to a larger network such as the Internet.
questions.explain: A switch handles traffic only inside the local network. Routing to a larger network such as the Internet is the router's job.
